en: Functional value equivalence is the criterion that judges whether a change to an Immaterial Object of Consumption has preserved, in substantial terms, what justified the purchase. The test rests on Article 51, item XIII, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, reaches the appearance of an item when appearance is what was bought, and leads to restoration.
If the platform may change, what does the law control in the change?

Every continuous digital service changes, and that fact is not in dispute. A change, taken in itself, is not unlawful, because the environment presupposes maintenance, improvement and adaptation, and updates may be necessary for compatibility, security, stability and legibility. The difficulty appears elsewhere, when the change stops working that way and begins to degrade, empty or divert, in a relevant way, the function that justified the purchase and structured the legitimate expectation of enjoyment.

The problem begins when it ceases to operate as a legitimate form of maintenance, improvement or adaptation of the supply and begins to degrade, empty or divert, in a relevant way, the function that justified the purchase and structured the legitimate expectation of enjoyment.<1>p. 729</1>
Updates may be necessary for compatibility, security, stability and legibility in a competitive ecosystem.<1>p. 470</1>

Faced with this, the debate tends to swing between two extremes. One treats any change as breach, and the other legitimizes every alteration by the operational continuity of the system or by the nominal survival of the object. Neither position holds, and the question changes. Instead of asking whether the change occurred within the supplier's general power to update, the interpreter asks whether, after it, the acquired experience remains functionally equivalent, in substantial terms, to the one that justified the object's entry into the user's sphere of consumption.
On one side, it rejects the claim to freeze the environment in a fixed state, as if any mutation automatically constituted breach.<1>p. 731</1>
On the other, it rejects the claim that every alteration would be legitimized by the mere operational continuity of the system or by the mere nominal survival of the object.<1>p. 731</1>
The legally relevant question then ceases to be whether the change occurred within the supplier's general power to update.<1>p. 730</1>

It becomes whether, after the alteration, the acquired experience remains functionally equivalent in substantial terms to the one that legitimized the object's entry into the user's sphere of consumption.<1>p. 730</1>

The category that answers this question is functional value equivalence, which serves at once as a criterion of comparison and of restoration. It places side by side the utility stabilized in the bond and the utility delivered after relevant modulations, the name given to the alterations the supplier makes in performing the service. Its counterpart is open auditability, treated in its own chapter. The first answers for the how much and the what of the change, and the second for the how. Each depends on the other, because without a verifiable minimum about what changed there is no rational basis for comparing promise and delivery, and without a criterion of comparison transparency shrinks to the ability to narrate changes.

Functional value equivalence designates the criterion of comparison and restoration by which one judges whether the utility delivered, after relevant modulations, substantially preserves the core of enjoyed utility, including when part of the value is structured by socially verifiable symbolic dimensions.<1>p. 469</1>

Once such a limit is set, functional value equivalence can be formulated as a criterion of comparison between the utility stabilized in the bond and the utility delivered after relevant modulations.<1>p. 478</1>

Without functional equivalence, auditability runs the risk of becoming transparency without material density, that is, a mere capacity to narrate changes without a criterion to assess their substantive legitimacy.<1>p. 638</1>
Why does the answer that the item is still there not close the case?

The supplier's first defense is usually that nothing was taken away, since the item remains in the inventory, the account remains active and the contract remains in force. A reading centered on abstract ownership or on the formal permanence of the asset would accept this answer, but it does not reach what is in dispute. Relevant alterations may keep the name, the general appearance and the nominal existence of the object and, even so, substantially compromise the enjoyment built into the bond. What the system protects is the integrity of enjoyment, and not the appearance that something is still there.

It is precisely for this reason that functional value equivalence presents itself as a more adequate parameter than a reading centered only on abstract ownership or on the formal permanence of the asset: what the system must protect is the integrity of enjoyment, and not the mere appearance that “something is still there”.<1>p. 648</1>

The permanence of the item, the functionality, the account, the access or the feature does not, by itself, neutralize the emptying of the experience if the concrete role of the object is degraded, diverted or made substantially different from the one that justified the purchase.<1>p. 730</1>

Consumer dogmatics already offers the path. Bruno Miragem treats liability for defects as the breach of a duty of adequacy, that is, of the quality the product or service must have to serve the ends legitimately expected of it, and he distinguishes the defect from absolute breach, because it corresponds to partial or imperfect performance. Benjamin, Marques and Bessa describe the functional defect as a nonconformity that prevents or limits the function for which the good is intended. With this support, once the legitimately expected utility has been emptied, the inadequacy is already given, even if the account remains active and the item remains listed.

Functional value equivalence can be upheld as a consumer-law criterion for the lawfulness of alterations because liability for defects arises from the breach of a duty of adequacy, that is, of the quality of the product or service to serve the ends legitimately expected of it.<1>p. 649</1>
The defect is not confused with absolute breach, but corresponds to partial or imperfect performance, aimed at satisfying the parties' interest in the very performance of the contract<1>p. 649</1>
The CDC works with the functional defect precisely to reach nonconformities that frustrate the consumer's legitimate expectation without requiring the total disappearance of the object<1>p. 652</1>
If the legitimately expected utility has been emptied, the inadequacy is already given, even if the account remains active and the item remains listed in the inventory<1>p. 653-654</1>

Rizzatto Nunes provides the image that serves as an objective yardstick, that of the supplier who cuts the classes of a course and keeps the same price. On platforms, the cut rarely appears as an explicit reduction. It may show up as loss of reach, persistent downgrading of performance, cumulative restriction of features, compression of limits, reordering of visibility or structural alterations that raise the cost of enjoying the same utility. The form changes, and the logic stays the same.
The label and the price are kept, and the delivery of value is lowered.<1>p. 480</1>

The reduction rarely appears as an explicit cut of “classes”, but may manifest itself as loss of reach, persistent downgrading of performance, cumulative restriction of features, compression of limits, reordering of visibility or structural alterations that raise the cost of enjoying the same utility.<1>p. 480</1>
Where does the criterion rest within the consumer system?

The first support is the reading of the contract as a process. Claudia Lima Marques sees the contract as a dynamic relationship, which is born, lives and dies, and she rejects the idea of an empty space between the birth of the obligation and the satisfaction of the main performance, because from the start the parties are bound by ancillary duties of conduct imposed by good faith. If the contract is a process, equivalence does not call for identity of means but for substantial continuity of the expected core of utility, which often requires active conduct from the supplier over time, and not the mere formal preservation of access. Marques also observes that long-term contracts carry an implicit expectation of changes, and this observation is read with its counterpart, so that changes are admitted when aimed at maintaining potential and quality, and not at the silent replacement of the object by a less valuable version.
If the contract is a process, equivalence does not require identity of means.<1>p. 478</1>
It requires substantial continuity of the expected core of utility, especially when the utility depends on a technical and organizational environment in continuous operation.<1>p. 478</1>

Marques rejects the idea of an empty space between the birth of the obligation and the satisfaction of the main performance, stating that the obligational relationship is a continuous whole.<1>p. 478</1>
In platform-governed enjoyment, preserving functional equivalence often requires active conduct over time, and not the mere formal preservation of access.<1>p. 478-479</1>

This formulation provides the fine fit for functional value equivalence: changes may be admissible and even necessary, provided they are aimed at maintaining the potential and the quality that structure the enjoyed utility, and not at the silent replacement of the object by a less valuable version.<1>p. 479</1>

The second support comes from continuing and dependent relationships. The parallel with long-term captive contracts, in which practical dependence ties the consumer to the bond, serves as disciplined interpretive infrastructure, and not as an automatic transplant. In these bonds what is protected is the minimum stability of the performance program and the trust built over time. Marques calls legitimate expectations the minimum objective basis of the consumer contract, and the expression calls for careful reading, because it does not authorize delivering the minimum. It designates that without which the relationship becomes unbalanced, so much so that excluding fundamental expectations makes the imbalance structural.
The parallel with long-term captive contracts does not enter here as an automatic transplant or as academic ornament, but as disciplined interpretive infrastructure.<1>p. 650</1>
In bonds of this nature, what is protected is not only the initial delivery, but the minimum stability of the performance program and the trust legitimately built over time<1>p. 650</1>

Legitimate expectations form the “minimum (objective) basis of the relationship, of the consumer contract”, so that, once these expectations are excluded, “the imbalance of the relationship is flagrant”<1>p. 648</1>
If the fundamental legitimate expectations that sustained the contracting are excluded, the imbalance is no longer a detail: it becomes structural<1>p. 653</1>

The third support is objective good faith in lasting relationships. Judith Martins-Costa treats it as a measure of lawfulness and as a brake, in specific cases, on the ius variandi, the power of one party to alter the performance alone, and she points to unfavorable surprise and the rupture of previously tolerated patterns as a breach of trust, even if the contract remains nominally in force. From her also comes the dynamic synallagma, the idea that contractual balance is not exhausted at the moment of agreement and accompanies the relationship over time. The point is decisive for the IOC, whose consumption does not happen only at purchase but over the course of enjoyment, so that the lawfulness of the alteration is measured by the functional unity of the relationship. Marques, Benjamin and Miragem add the creative function of good faith, a source of new ancillary duties and of professional risks that cannot be disposed of by contract, and among them are the risks of technical obsolescence, compatibility mutations and structural reconfigurations.

Objective good faith functions expressly as a measure for assessing lawfulness in the exercise of rights derived from legal transactions, including to set the limits of the exercise of termination in lasting contracts of continued performance and to impose brakes on the ius variandi in specific cases<1>p. 650</1>

Unfavorable and harmful surprise, the abrupt rupture of previously tolerated patterns and the abrupt reconfiguration of the expected utility may constitute a breach of trust and a violation of the contractual program concretely lived, even if the contract remains nominally in force<1>p. 650-651</1>
There is also a dynamic synallagma, that is, a functional balance that accompanies the relationship over time<1>p. 651</1>

Therefore, the lawfulness of the alteration must be assessed in light of the functional unity of the relationship, and not only of the abstract existence of a generic authorization to change.<1>p. 651</1>

The consequence is plain, since, if continued performance exposes the consumer to risks of technical obsolescence, compatibility mutations and structural reconfigurations, good faith must require care, cooperation and maintenance as duties to preserve functional equivalence, and thus impose liability when trust is broken by reconfigurations that degrade, in a relevant and persistent way, the core of utility.<1>p. 479</1>

The fourth support is the offer. For Miragem, the consumer decides to contract in view of the advantages and qualities offered, and from this arises the legal duty to maintain the offered conditions or, at least, to substantially preserve their utility. With these supports together, the category does not appear as a new right placed beside the CDC. It organizes, for the case of alterations, duties the Code itself already contains, and so the charge of invention finds its answer in Karl Larenz's description of the legal system as open and, to a certain degree, mobile, calling for functional concretization when the factual basis shifts.
Functional value equivalence is an outgrowth of good faith, of the binding force of the offer and of the protection of trust within the CDC.<1>p. 652</1>

The offer and the trust it awakens offer a direct basis for this identification, since the consumer contracts in view of the advantages and qualities advertised, from which arises the legal duty to maintain the offered conditions or, at least, to substantially preserve their utility<1>p. 652</1>
This move also protects the construction against the objection of “inventing” law, because the legal system is open and requires functional concretization when the factual basis shifts.<1>p. 481</1>
What does Article 51, item XIII, of the CDC reach?

Article 51, item XIII, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> declares null and void the clauses that authorize the supplier to unilaterally modify the content or quality of the contract after it is concluded. Commenting on it, Nunes asks how it could be possible to alter a contract alone and still give validity to the alteration. Benjamin, Marques and Bessa say that a clause giving the supplier the prerogative to innovate unilaterally clashes with contractual balance, and Miragem explains why, which is the concentration in the supplier of the power to direct the relationship, with the consumer reduced to a spectator.
For this reason, the CDC treats the unilateral modification of content or quality as nullity.<1>p. 479</1>

Any modification of the consumer contract must observe bilaterality and the absence of abusive imposition, so that a clause arming the supplier with the prerogative to innovate unilaterally in the relationship clashes with contractual balance, its validity being undermined by art. 51, XIII<1>p. 654</1>

Clauses that authorize the supplier to unilaterally modify the content or quality of the contract after its conclusion are abusive, precisely because they concentrate in the supplier the power to direct the relationship and reduce the consumer to a mere spectator of the course of the transaction<1>p. 651-652</1>

The provision speaks of a clause, and carrying it over to conduct calls for care. With Miragem, unilateral alteration is already enough, by itself, to characterize abusiveness, but this statement concerns the clauses that authorize the change and cannot be repeated without that limit, as if every alteration were unlawful. Outside that limit, unilateral alteration is, by itself, legally sensitive, the problem does not lie in every change considered in the abstract, and what is refused is the mutation imposed without the consumer's effective participation, without preserving balance and without respect for the functional core of enjoyment.

If unilateral alteration is already enough, by itself, to characterize abusiveness, this characteristic is aggravated when the content of the change results in the reduction or impairment of the consumer's interest in the performance<1>p. 652</1>

Unilateral alteration is already, by itself, legally sensitive in the CDC; and this sensitivity is aggravated when the change is not neutral, but results in a material reduction or impairment of the consumer's interest in the performance<1>p. 651-652</1>

The problem does not lie in every change considered in the abstract, but in the mutation imposed without the consumer's effective participation, without preserving the balance of the relationship and without respect for the functional core of enjoyment.<1>p. 654</1>

The lawyer therefore faces two different questions. The first concerns the clause, and the answer is that the lawfulness of the change is not measured by its abstract provision in the contract, so that a generic authorization to alter does not offer the defense the supplier seeks. The second concerns the concrete alteration, which is judged by the equivalence test. On this level, a relevant unilateral modification, when untethered from restoration and from the substantial preservation of use value, ceases to be mere management of the service and begins to approach structural abusiveness. The verb is approach, and it is worth keeping.
The lawfulness of the mutation is not measured by its mere abstract provision in a contractual clause, nor by the formal permanence of the object after the alteration.<1>p. 650</1>

A relevant unilateral modification, when untethered from restoration and from the substantial preservation of use value, ceases to be mere management of the service and begins to approach structural abusiveness<1>p. 654</1>
How is the test applied?

The test opens only in the face of an alteration with the potential to affect in a relevant way the practical function, the position in the ecosystem, the symbolic density or the continuity of enjoyment of the object. Any minor change, visual touch-up or marginal fluctuation typical of the normal life of the service stays outside. The trigger appears when the platform carries out a downgrading of use, limitation of access, loss of compatibility, alteration of essential parameters, removal of features, structural rebalancing, discontinuation of a role in the ecosystem, degradation of relational position or emptying of attributes with objective weight in the rationale of the purchase.

Its field of application opens whenever there is an alteration with the potential to affect in a relevant way the practical function, the ecosystemic position, the symbolic density or the continuity of enjoyment of the IOC.<1>p. 651</1>
The trigger is not any minor change, any visual touch-up or any marginal fluctuation typical of the normal life of the service.<1>p. 651</1>

The standard switches on when the platform carries out a downgrading of use, limitation of access, loss of compatibility, alteration of essential parameters, removal of features, structural rebalancing, discontinuation of an ecosystemic role, degradation of relational position or emptying of attributes with objective weight in the rationale of the purchase<1>p. 651</1>

The examination is structured in four steps. The first identifies the functional core of the object and asks what practical utility justified the purchase, what role the object played in the ecosystem and, where pertinent, what symbolic, reputational or relational density was objectively built into the enjoyment. The analysis is neither psychologizing nor folkloric. What is sought is a verifiable core that formed part of the legitimately formed expectation, and the offer, with the trust it awakened, is the direct basis for reconstructing it.
It does not matter whether the consumer “loved” that item.<1>p. 652</1>
The first step consists in identifying the functional core of the object.<1>p. 652</1>
Where pertinent, what symbolic, reputational or relational density was objectively built into the enjoyment?<1>p. 652</1>
What matters is whether there was a verifiable core of utility, role and meaning that formed part of the legitimately formed expectation<1>p. 652</1>

The second step reconstructs the alteration and the impact, comparing before and after in use, performance, access, compatibility, function in the ecosystem, recognition, rarity, trajectory or continuity of experience. It is in this step that the dependence on auditability shows itself in practice. When the platform prevents the reconstruction of the impact, opacity ceases to be neutral and turns into a dogmatic aggravating factor, that is, a factor that worsens the supplier's position in the examination, because it makes it impossible to control adequacy and the very legitimacy of the change. This control cannot depend on the chance that the consumer archived evidence or has the technical knowledge to produce homemade comparisons.
Functional equivalence without auditability becomes an elegant guess.<1>p. 653</1>
The second step is to reconstruct the alteration and the impact.<1>p. 652</1>
What is the before and after in terms of use, performance, access, compatibility, ecosystemic function, recognition, rarity, trajectory or continuity of experience?<1>p. 652</1>
If the platform prevents reconstruction of the impact, opacity is not neutral.<1>p. 653</1>
It turns into a dogmatic aggravating factor, because it makes it impossible to control adequacy, trust and the very legitimacy of the mutation.<1>p. 653</1>

The third step measures the relevance of the loss and separates the marginal loss, part of the ordinary evolution of the service, from the substantial emptying of the functional core. Not every reduction is unlawful, but there is a point beyond which the alteration ceases to be ordinary adaptation and begins to operate as a material downgrading of the acquired use value. Equivalence works here as a yardstick of relevance, which distinguishes ordinary variation from substantial and persistent downgrading.
Platforms are not wax museums.<1>p. 653</1>
The third step is to measure the relevance of the loss.<1>p. 653</1>
Not every reduction is unlawful.<1>p. 653</1>

Equivalence works as a yardstick of relevance, since it turns the discussion about change into a discussion about preserving a core, distinguishing ordinary variation from substantial and persistent downgrading.<1>p. 478</1>

The fourth step examines justification and restoration, because even a relevant loss may be legally tolerable if there is verifiable justification and adequate restoration. One asks whether the platform demonstrated, in a minimally auditable way, the technical or systemic reason for the change and whether it offered real alternatives, such as reversibility, a parallel version, equivalent functional replacement, correction of parameters, preservation of compatibility or restoration of status. It is not enough to acknowledge the change and assert one's own power to make it. In the end the examination comes down to three questions, which are whether the alteration substantially preserved the functional, ecosystemic and, when relevant, symbolic core of enjoyment, whether there was verifiable justification and whether there was adequate restoration.
The fourth step is to examine justification and restoration.<1>p. 653</1>
Even when there is a relevant loss, the mutation may still be legally tolerable if there is verifiable justification and adequate restoration.<1>p. 653</1>
Thus, it is not enough merely to acknowledge the change and assert one's own power to carry it out.<1>p. 653</1>
Contrary to such caricatures, it offers a finer criterion: did the alteration substantially preserve the functional, ecosystemic and, when relevant, symbolic core of enjoyment?<1>p. 655</1>

This test does not measure minimum utility, and the word functional tends to lead to that error. Equivalence is not reduced to maintaining technical performance in the strict sense nor to the quantitative preservation of isolated attributes, and its content is more demanding. What is compared is the role of the object in the acquired experience, considering its concrete utility in the ecosystem, its relational place in the environment of use and, when legally relevant, its identity or symbolic density. That is why the question is not whether the platform kept offering something under the same label, nor whether the object still serves some purpose, but whether it keeps serving, at a functionally equivalent level, the ends that justified contracting and maintaining the relationship. Functional value also does not coincide with efficiency measurable by linear indicators, because it is usually constituted by the object's position in the trajectory of enjoyment, by the kind of interaction it allows and by the way it connects with the rest of the ecosystem.
Functional value equivalence is not reduced to maintaining technical performance in the strict sense, nor to the quantitative preservation of isolated attributes.<1>p. 729</1>
Its content is more demanding.<1>p. 729</1>
In all these cases, the decisive question must not be whether the platform kept offering “something” under the same label.<1>p. 638</1>

In other words, the legally relevant question is not whether everything remained identical, but whether the object keeps serving, at a functionally equivalent level, the ends that legitimately justified contracting and maintaining the relationship<1>p. 649</1>
In immaterial objects of consumption, functional value does not necessarily coincide with operational efficiency measurable by linear indicators.<1>p. 729</1>

It is often constituted also by the position the object occupies in the consumer's trajectory of enjoyment, by the kind of interaction it allows, by the way it connects with other parts of the ecosystem and by the practical meaning it takes on in the acquired experience.<1>p. 729</1>
When does the symbolic enter the comparison?

Functional value comprises capacity of use, performance, access and compatibility, and may reach the object's role in the ecosystem, its relational relevance, its position of use, its density of rarity, its function of distinction and the way it forms part of trajectory, status and recognition. In governed environments, certain symbolic and positional dimensions are not accessories, because they are part of the utility for which the consumer joins, stays and invests. The condition is that they form part, in a verifiable way, of the promised core of enjoyment, or, in the wording of the parameter, that they make up in an objectively recognizable way the core of the purchase. Outside that, there is no legal claim, and touchiness dressed up as dogmatics is not accepted.

This includes, for example, capacity of use, performance, access and compatibility, but may also reach the role of the object within the ecosystem, its relational relevance, its position of use, its density of rarity, its function of distinction or the way it forms part of trajectory, status and recognition stabilized in the environment<1>p. 649</1>
When these elements form part, in a verifiable way, of the promised core of enjoyment, their degradation may be legally relevant even if the object remains formally accessible<1>p. 650</1>

In these cases, functional equivalence may also require preserving the relational and symbolic density of enjoyment, provided that this dimension makes up, in an objectively recognizable way, the core of the purchase.<1>p. 730-731</1>
The point is not to turn every subjective preference into a legal claim, nor to open the door to touchiness dressed up as dogmatics.<1>p. 649</1>

The lock against psychologism comes from Umberto Eco. For him, the symbolic dimension is described as cultural correlation, formulated in terms that do not depend on the association made by a particular mind, and the code operates with coercive value once stabilized by social use. This reading carries over to digital ecosystems, in which signs, metrics, badges, rarities, rankings and visibility regimes operate as coercive relations of the environment itself, to which the consumer is subject by taking part. Hence the practical consequence that symbolic losses can be described by public criteria, without any need to ask the consumer what he or she felt. The relevant expectation is authorized and induced by the code, and not idiosyncratic. This opening does not authorize turning any symbolic value into an indeterminate obligation, because the examination isolates what was an operative condition of that specific position and compares whether this core was preserved.

Thus, the objection of mentalism does not hold because we are not speaking of associations or mental images, but of correlations formulated in cultural terms, which refer to one another on an abstractly cultural plane, regardless of whether a human mind makes that association<1>p. 477</1>
In digital ecosystems, signs, metrics, badges, rarities, rankings and visibility regimes do not function as a subjective ornament added to the “real product”.<1>p. 477</1>
The consequence, for equivalence, is that symbolic losses can be described by public criteria.<1>p. 478</1>
The expectation is not idiosyncratic, but authorized and induced by code.<1>p. 478</1>

This does not authorize turning any symbolic value into an indeterminate legal obligation; on the contrary, it requires isolating what was relevant to that specific position and comparing whether the restoration preserved this core or merely kept signs of continuity while shifting, from within, what mattered.<1>p. 327</1>
How are the passages on aesthetic alteration reconciled?

Three formulations on aesthetics seem to point in different directions, and the lawyer will find each of them cited against the other. In the delimitation of the IOC, predominantly aesthetic alterations fall, as a rule, outside the concept, except when they make up a convergent set of signs capable of supporting the objective recognition of an unlawful act of architecture, through structural indications of abusive teleology. In the formulation of equivalence, mere aesthetic preference for an old experience is excluded. Between these two formulations, however, the update of visual effects on old cosmetics appears as an expressive example of the requirement of equivalence, with outcomes such as refund, credit or exchange.

A technically simple and dogmatically expressive example of this requirement of equivalence appears in the updates of visual effects on old cosmetics, carried out under the label of modernizing the game.<1>p. 469</1>

The reconciliation is made through the core that was sold, and the delimitation itself offers the key. The limit falls on functionally accessory symbolic value, which does not form part of the core of the promised bundle, and its function is to prevent the use of the regime to contest alterations incapable of reaching the core of the value offered. What decides, therefore, is not the visual character of the change, but the relation between what changed and what was sold. The three formulations do not appear together in a single sentence, and the reconciliation results from reading them together.
The function of this limit is to block the unmotivated use of the IOC regime to contest alterations incapable of depredating the core of the value offered.<1>p. 434</1>

Three hypotheses result from this reading. When appearance is accessory to the utility offered, the alteration stays, as a rule, outside. When the item is sold for the visual experience itself and for public distinction, and it is this core that the alteration downgrades, the change goes through the yardstick of equivalence, because the visual, in that item, is the acquired utility. In either case, a taste for the old version, with no verifiable core behind it, does not count. The proviso of the convergent set opens a distinct path, in which the aesthetic alteration, insufficient by itself, weighs as a sign within a set, and the examination moves to abusive teleology, treated in its own chapter. In practice, the lawyer's work lies in demonstrating what was sold, through the offer and the price, instead of insisting that the new version got worse.

It includes the way the item presents itself in the game space, the clarity with which it communicates an ability, the consistency of the visual “weight” the user experiences when triggering effects, and also the public distinction the cosmetic produces compared with common versions.<1>p. 469-470</1>

The dimension does not form part of it when it is a matter of aesthetics, marketing, generic advertising narrative or diffuse satisfaction with no identifiable functional core and no structural link to the sustained position of enjoyment.<1>p. 432</1>

It forms part of the bundle when it makes up the core of utility economically offered and enjoyed as a position in the ecosystem, that is, when the platform sells, explicitly or functionally, effects of recognition, visibility, circulation, reputation, belonging or status as part of the value of what is acquired.<1>p. 432</1>
What does the update of a cosmetic's visual effects show?

Riot Games carries out updates of visual effects on old cosmetics. In an environment where enjoyment depends on visual signals, legibility and social recognition, the value of the cosmetic is not exhausted by its presence in the inventory. It includes the way the item appears in the game, the clarity with which it communicates an ability, the visual weight the user experiences when triggering effects and the public distinction compared with common versions. When this set is persistently altered, the answer that the item is still there does not settle equivalence.

The case is useful because the company's justification is public and reasonable. In its own text, it describes the program as aimed at consistency, legibility and graphic quality, with objectives ranked by importance, and it states that the legibility of the mechanics will prevail over thematic resonance. The pursuit of clarity is not being contested, and the measure is understandable and may be desirable from the standpoint of the ecosystem. The problem lies elsewhere, because applying these criteria may, in specific cases, reconfigure the core that motivated the purchase. It does not follow that any given update was unlawful. The case shows where the legal question lies.

In making its criteria explicit, the text includes ranked objectives and a hierarchy of importance, holding that one of the objectives is to “reduce overall visual noise”, for example by “reducing the ‘invasion’ of textures that have many fine and unnecessary details”, and also stating that the objectives are “ranked in order of importance”, so that “the legibility of the game mechanics will always prevail over thematic resonance”<1>p. 470</1>
It is understandable and, from the standpoint of the ecosystem, may be desirable.<1>p. 470-471</1>

The next difficulty is one of proof. The Terms of Service take mutability as the rule, including for virtual products, and provide for background updating, with or without prior notice. The patch notes, in turn, serve for general information, but were not designed as a comparison tool for someone who needs to demonstrate the degradation of a specific cosmetic. The platform holds the history of decisions, versions and criteria, and the consumer receives fragments.
In addition, it is provided that the company may “use background patches” to automatically update games and software “with or without prior notice”<1>p. 470</1>

The way out is moderate and does not call for freezing the game. If the alteration preserves the core of utility, performance continues. If it downgrades in a relevant way what structured the utility for that consumer, restoration must include, at least, choice mechanisms that prevent captivity by surprise. Among the alternatives are refund, credit, exchange for another cosmetic of equivalent value or similar forms of recovering the investment, without requiring from the consumer the impossible proof of a black box. Modernization remains possible, and what is prevented is that the update imposes on the consumer a version he or she had no reason to expect as the new basis of enjoyment.
If the alteration preserves the core of utility, performance continues.<1>p. 471</1>

If the alteration downgrades in a relevant way what structured the utility for that consumer, restoration must include, at least, choice mechanisms that prevent captivity by surprise, with alternatives such as refund, credit, exchange for another cosmetic of equivalent value or similar forms of recovering the investment for the consumer's reinsertion in the ecosystem, without requiring from the consumer the impossible proof of a black box.<1>p. 471</1>

This design keeps the dialogue open and preserves the possibility of modernization, while preventing “update” from working as a label to impose on the consumer a version he or she had no reason to expect would be the new basis of enjoyment.<1>p. 471</1>
What do the nerf and the software update have in common?

The nerf is the technically deliberate weakening of attributes, abilities or items, made through an update, to make something less powerful in the practical working of the game. It is a downgrading of power in terms that are comparable and measurable in the environment, and among these terms are the stats, the numerical attributes that parameterize an object's performance, such as damage, resistance and speed. Abusive teleology and the unlawful act of architecture

Abusive teleology is the category of unlawful act of architecture that makes it possible to impute to the supplier a program of exploitation inscribed in the design of the service, when no clause and no isolated episode is enough to show the injury. It operates through five cumulative requirements, separates aggressive business from exploitative purpose and enters the CDC through doors the law has already opened.
What injury escapes when one looks only at the clause and the episode?

Change, alone, is not the problem. In a continuous digital service, altering, updating, rebalancing and reorganizing enjoyment is part of the way of supplying, and mutability, by itself, does not characterize unlawfulness. The problem begins when it ceases to maintain the consumed object and begins to function as an ordinary technique for exploiting vulnerability, obscuring understanding, concentrating proof in the supplier and reducing the possibility of reversing the bond.
The mutability of the service, by itself, is not enough to characterize unlawfulness.<1>p. 663</1>

The legal problem begins when this mutability ceases to operate as a legitimate form of maintaining the consumed object and begins to function as an ordinary technique of exploiting vulnerability, obscuring understanding, unilaterally concentrating proof and systematically reducing the reversibility of the bond.<1>p. 663</1>

This passage rarely leaves a mark in a single place. Many exploitative architectures do not produce spectacular harm, but ordinary wear, diffuse loss and selective difficulty, made of small pressures that, taken separately, seem tolerable roughness of the environment. The law was trained more to react to delimited events than to programs of operation, and from this arise two insufficient responses. The first dissolves the conflict in the language of innovation or of the dynamic nature of the platform, as if continuous reorganization immunized any downgrading. The second reduces control to hunting isolated clauses, as if the supply could only be examined in its textual fragments.
Many exploitative architectures do not produce a spectacular harm-event.<1>p. 733</1>
They produce ordinary wear, diffuse loss, selective difficulty, progressive obscuring and silent reconfiguration of the experience.<1>p. 733</1>
The law tends, at times, to underestimate these forms of injury because it was historically trained more to react to delimited events than to programs of operation.<1>p. 733</1>

The first would be to dissolve the problem in the vague language of “innovation” or of the “dynamic nature” of the platform, as if the continuous reorganization of the environment were enough to immunize any relevant downgrading of enjoyment.<1>p. 664</1>

The second would be to reduce the legal response to the atomized hunt for isolated clauses, as if the supply could only be controlled in its textual fragments and never in its operational logic.<1>p. 664</1>

Abusiveness shifts from the event to the regime. Clauses, one-off acts and specific failures remain relevant, but may be only localized manifestations of an orientation built into the ordinary operation of the ecosystem. When governance repeatedly organizes informational noise, decisional friction, evidentiary opacity, mutation that does not lend itself to audit and insufficient restoration, the unlawful act no longer lies only in the wording of the contract, because it lies in the architecture. This shift fits within the grammar of the CDC and needs no parallel law for platforms.
If enjoyment is governed, the way of governing it must also remain subject to criteria of legitimacy.<1>p. 664</1>

When this governance repeatedly organizes informational noise, decisional friction, evidentiary opacity, non-auditable mutation and insufficient restoration, the unlawful act no longer lies only in the wording.<1>p. 664</1>
With this, abusiveness ceases to be thought only on the scale of the isolated event and comes to be thought on the scale of the regime.<1>p. 664</1>

The names call for clarification. Three expressions cover the same field, unlawful act of architecture, unlawful act of abusive teleology and teleological unlawful act of architecture, and they do not always come separated. The clearest relation is that of abusive teleology as a category of unlawful act of architecture, that is, as a mode of imputation that reaches exploitative purposes inscribed in the technical and organizational design of the service, and not only in contractual commands. It is also not to be confused with the law of the platform, which is a descriptive category of the setting in which power is exercised, while abusive teleology is a category of imputation. Its formulation depends on two prior categories, because there is no capturable unlawful act without the semiotic vulnerability it exploits, nor without the enjoyment bundle, the utility acquired and sustained over time, that it degrades.

As long as the design is perceived as a neutral technical setting, it stays outside imputation. The starting point is Julie Cohen, who describes governance by architecture as the capacity of protocols and centralized controls to actively define the space of possibilities of enjoyment, and modulation as the permanent adjustment of the environment through information flows. What does the five-requirement test consist of?

Abusive teleology is defined as the structural deviation of platform-governed supply in which architecture and governance come to operate oriented by an identifiable exploitative purpose, with patterns of modulation that degrade, reconfigure or condition enjoyment beyond the ordinary risk of continued performance. Its object is the architectural program, the set of repeated choices that organizes possibilities, introduces frictions, manages visibilities, distributes sanctions and stabilizes dependencies. So as not to become an elastic label, the qualification takes the form of a test of cumulative elements, so that the absence of one of them is enough to rule it out.

With the premises and their respective limits established, abusive teleology can be defined, at this point, as the structural deviation of platform-governed supply in which the architecture and governance of the environment come to operate in a way oriented by an identifiable exploitative purpose, producing and reinforcing patterns of modulation that degrade, reconfigure or condition enjoyment beyond the ordinary risk of continued performance.<1>p. 448</1>

For this qualification to remain controllable and not turn into an elastic label, it must take the form of a test made up of cumulative elements, able to bring the discussion back to verifiable requirements and to delimit the edges of application.<1>p. 448</1>

The first requirement is inscribed teleology. The exploitative purpose must be reconstructable as something built into design choices, terms of use, authorization mechanisms and enforcement strategies, a word that designates the application of rules by the supplier itself, and not as an occasional side effect.
