What is controlled is not an inner will, but a recognizable program of operation.<1>p. 732</1>
This qualification does not depend on proving the supplier's inner psychological intent, as if the unlawful act required a subjective confession of malice.<1>p. 668</1>

It names cases in which the architecture of the service was conceived or came to be administered so as to structurally exploit the consumer's vulnerability, turning opacity, friction, difficulty of reversal, capture of expectation and concentration of proof into ordinary elements of performance.<1>p. 669</1>

Proof of the exploitative character does not depend on a subjective reading, because the institutional material itself describes the structure in terms of probability, progression and guarantees by attempts, in addition to presenting a spending cap.<1>p. 450</1>

There is, however, a tension the lawyer needs to know, because the other side may exploit it. In a presentational register, abusive teleology appears as the worst of design defects, which intentionally precedes the harm and the program, and, when deliberate, it ceases to be a failure and becomes method. Read alone, these sentences suggest a subjective element. The requirements of the test say the opposite, and the category is described by the method of exploitation built into the supply regime, without speaking of will. What decides are the requirements, because it is in them that the category operates as a criterion, and deliberation is the clearest case, not a condition for application. The lack of proof of intent, therefore, does not rule out the qualification.
The rationality of the program is legally more important than the benevolent self-description the platform makes of itself.<1>p. 668</1>
It is the worst of design defects, since it intentionally precedes the harm and the program.<1>p. 32</1>
When deliberate, it ceases to be a failure and becomes method.<1>p. 32</1>

Its meaning lies in identifying situations in which opacity, friction, manufactured urgency, selective reconfiguration, asymmetry of reversal and normalization of small losses cease to be episodic occurrences and come to make up a method of exploitation built into the supply regime itself.<1>p. 794</1>
What do the Sanctum and the Exalted skins allow us to discuss?

The case arises from a trait of the supplier, which is an entertainment company and can extend the playful frame beyond the product, so that buying, converting currency, deciphering price and following event windows become game mechanics themselves. The transposition is not symmetrical, and so the claim that it is a game works as a symptom, and not as a justification, when the mechanic bears on contracting and enjoyment, and not on the content delivered.

Unlike a stage of the game, whose rules exist so that the player can, in theory, beat them, the game embedded in the consumer relationship is designed and refereed by the supplier itself, which defines the probabilities, sets the unit of account, recalibrates the internal exchange rate and establishes the deadlines, systematically reserving for itself the position of the house.<1>p. 449</1>

For this reason, the claim that "it is a game" does not operate, here, as a justification, but as a symptom: when the playful mechanic is applied to contracting and enjoyment themselves, and not to the content delivered, it comes to indicate the deviation of purpose instead of dispelling it.<1>p. 449</1>

The facts come from Riot Games' own material. The Exalted skins were presented as a layer of exclusivity at the top of the League of Legends catalog, and access to them goes through the Sanctum, a store where the player buys a currency of its own, at 400 RP per unit, RP being the game's paid points. With it, the player enters draws, with a very low chance, a guarantee only on the eightieth draw and availability for a limited time. The result is a cap of 32,000 RP, against 3,250 RP for an Ultimate skin, the previously known tier, or about 9.85 times. In reais, the calculation reaches something close to R$ 102.80 and R$ 911.60 in typical purchase arrangements, figures that serve as demonstration, and not as a single price. Those who do not receive the main item usually receive currency and collateral cosmetics.

The official description of the Sanctum records that Exalted skins are the only Tier S content of the corresponding banner, with an extremely low chance and a guarantee only on the eightieth draw, in addition to availability for a limited time <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025d)</2>.<3>p. 299</3>

The Exalted, in turn, operates by attempts at 400 RP per Ancient Sparks, with a guarantee by the eightieth attempt, which sets a cap of [80 × 400 RP = 32,000 RP] <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024g; Riot Games, 2025d)</2>.<3>p. 301</3>

The use here is demonstrative of the economic asymmetry produced by the engineering of access, and not the setting of a single invariable price in all possible combinations <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024c)</2>.<3>p. 301</3>

This economic tie is not made through a declared obligation of joint purchase, but through the design of the path, in which most results do not deliver the desired good and come back as intermediate rewards, especially currency and collateral cosmetics, which come to work as symbolic cushions for the spending and as an incentive to keep trying <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024a)</2>.<3>p. 450</3>

The reading of the case is strong and points to a functional tying sale, in which the direct purchase of the main good is barred, the consumer finances along the way a diffuse package of other items and comes to pay to try, on a path that replaces the mode of acquisition instead of running beside it. The jump in cost, in turn, comes mainly from scarcity, rotation and limited time, and not from a necessarily superior material jump. For the fourth and fifth requirements, however, this examination is still to be done, because the Sanctum illustrates mainly the third requirement, and the case does not go through the five one by one.

This design makes explicit a relevant loss of the consumer's autonomy, who no longer chooses the means of access to the good and comes to “pay to try”, with accumulated progression and a foreseen spending cap, in a logic that is only completed with continued consumption in the system itself <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024a)</2>.<3>p. 450</3>

In this key, innovation does not operate as a parallel alternative, but as a replacement of the mode of acquisition, conditioning the enjoyment of the main good on accepting an exploitative architecture of calculated risk<1>p. 450</1>

In the Sanctum, however, the jump in cost is produced mainly by scarcity, rotation and limited time, while the increase in content remains, in essence, within the grammar that historically already organized the top of the catalog <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024g; Riot Games, 2025d)</2>.<3>p. 301-302</3>

The provisos decide the reach of the case. The problem depends on the removal of the direct purchase, because it would not exist if the option to acquire the skin at a proportional and reasonable price were kept, and the mandatory path comes closer to an abusive practice of tying than to an entertainment experience attentive to users' expectations. Nor is it a matter of moralizing the draw model itself. The accumulated progression and the spending cap are facts of the case, which serve as proof of the design, and must enter any honest analysis. What the case offers the lawyer is a possible reading, useful for showing how purpose is reconstructed from documents, and not a conclusion about the company, which would depend on the full demonstration of the test.
It would not be a problem if the option of directly purchasing the skin at a proportional and reasonable price were kept.<1>p. 450</1>

However, by making the path mandatory, the company comes closer to an abusive practice of tying than to the creation of an entertainment experience that truly cares about the expectations and wishes of its consumer users.<1>p. 450-451</1>
Where do the Runes, the Prestige skins and the Eternals stand on this threshold?

The Runes are the negative control. The reform rewrote the system of pre-match choices, and still it is not organized as exploitation, because the new set came with no direct charge and imposed neither relevant loss nor a mandatory spending route. The criterion appears in the contrast, since the modulation would turn into a deviation of purpose if the reform had extinguished the previous investment without equivalent restoration and required compulsory purchase. The same logic applies to the hypothetical bundle sold as complete, with an objective promise of future content, if the platform later removed that attribute and required a new purchase.
The existence of this kind of architecture does not authorize concluding that every deep reprogramming of the service constitutes abusive teleology.<1>p. 451</1>

If the reform had extinguished the previous investment without an equivalent means of restoration, and if the new system required compulsory purchase or prevented the user from preserving the position of enjoyment that motivated past spending, the modulation would cease to be compatible with the purpose of consumption and would come to constitute a deviation of purpose.<1>p. 452</1>
In this configuration, the platform not only changes the environment, but rebuilds the relationship to extract again what had already been built into the consumer's expectation.<1>p. 452</1>

The Prestige skins show that the loss may not be functional. Their value rested, at least when the regime was introduced, on institutionally managed scarcity, and the conflict arises when items treated as rare return to the market. Riot Games announced that the original holders would receive exclusive modified versions, in recognition of their investment, and this note is an indication that the company itself treats status as part of enjoyment and admits that a change of architecture may require restoration. It is an illustration of the threshold, and the restoration sought to preserve the differential of distinction, or at least to justify it narratively and partially. The deviation only becomes identifiable when the reorganization is a relevant loss without an equivalent means, or when the restoration is insufficient to maintain the core that justified the purchase.

The institutional response is, methodologically, the most important part of the conflict, because, in the case in question, it is able to confirm, from the company's own statements, that status is a material component of enjoyment and that, when the architecture changes, there may be a need for restoration.<1>p. 453</1>

Here, the relevance does not lie in the “cosmetic curiosity”, but in the institutional reasoning, since the restoration proposed by the developer itself sought to preserve - or, at least narratively, partially justify - a differential of distinction exactly where the change threatened to injure<1>p. 453</1>

The Eternals are a test case, and not because they are already abusive. The institutional offer describes the pass as a purchase that reaches future champions, so that continuity forms part of the bundle by the supplier's word, and not by the consumer's hope. The deviation would only arise in a specific hypothesis, if the system were redesigned to remove that attribute and require a new purchase. New series and ordinary adjustments would not fall within it, and contractual elasticity, alone, would not settle the question.

In parallel, the Eternals regime is suited to serve as a test case for delimiting the threshold between legitimate modulation and abusive teleology, not because it is already abusive, but because the institutional offer itself describes the pass as a purchase with a projection of future completeness, that is, as a good whose utility is not exhausted in the present content.<1>p. 454</1>

The point would not be the creation of new series or ordinary adjustments of the ecosystem, but a redesign that turned continuity, previously communicated as a component of the bundle, into compulsory recurrence, shifting the practical purpose of the purchase <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2022g)</2>.<3>p. 454</3>

Contractual elasticity, in isolation, therefore does not solve the problem, since, if the offer incorporated the future projection as the core of the good, a retroactive removal of this core could constitute a relevant loss without equivalent restoration, characterizing a deviation of purpose <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 455</3>
How can aggressive business be told apart from exploitative purpose?

Commercial aggressiveness is not the criterion. Abusive teleology is not to be confused with a business choice that is merely harsh, with debatable design or with an architecture simply efficient for the supplier, and imputation cannot arise from discomfort with the business model nor from criticism of the existence of monetization, engagement or curation. Capture techniques are also not of interest as a moral catalog of aggressive strategies. A business may be tough, expensive and unappealing without this making it unlawful.
In this key, abusive teleology is not to be confused with a business choice that is merely harsh, with debatable design or with an architecture simply efficient for the supplier.<1>p. 666</1>
The imputation of abusive teleology cannot arise from vague discomfort with the business model nor from intuitive criticism of the existence of monetization, engagement or curation.<1>p. 734</1>

Techniques of capture through scarcity, risk and dependence are not of interest here as a moral catalog of “aggressive strategies” nor as a sociological inventory of engagement mechanisms.<1>p. 670</1>

The separation is made by questions that the cases and the test allow one to draw out. The first is whether the effect arises from the design itself or is an occasional consequence of performance. The second is whether it repeats as a regularity or is an episode. The third is whether there is an equivalent route, such as direct purchase at a proportional price in the Sanctum case, free access in the Runes case or sufficient restoration, because its absence weighs when continued use becomes a new mandatory spending route. The fourth is whether the consumer can understand and contest what happened. The fifth is whether the dominant orientation of the arrangement is exploitation or a legitimate purpose, such as security, stability and balance.

There are structural reforms that rewrite the environment of enjoyment and, even so, are not organized as exploitation, precisely because they impose no relevant loss nor turn continued use into a new mandatory spending route.<1>p. 451</1>
The deviation cannot be an isolated episode, a contingent error or an operational exception.<1>p. 448</1>
It is not enough that the system be complex or operate with metrics.<1>p. 455</1>

The supplier may invoke these purposes, and the argument carries weight, but claims of efficiency, optimization, system balance or need for updating are not enough, by themselves, to neutralize control. The analysis goes beyond the rhetoric of technical necessity and asks about the practical purpose of the arrangement. In the end, the question ceases to be whether the platform may or may not change and becomes whether the design of the supply is compatible with good faith, balance, auditability, functional equivalence and a real possibility of reaction. The resulting limit is objective, because the architecture may organize enjoyment, provided it does not do so as a stable program of exploitation.
For this reason, claims of efficiency, optimization, system balance, operational convenience or need for updating are not enough, by themselves, to neutralize control.<1>p. 733</1>
The parameter does not serve to turn every intense architecture into an unlawful act.<1>p. 734</1>

From there, the discussion ceases to revolve around the impoverished question of whether the platform “may or may not change” and comes to bear on what really matters: whether the design of the supply was organized in a way compatible with good faith, balance, auditability, functional equivalence and a real possibility of reaction by the consumer.<1>p. 669</1>

What opens, then, is not an impressionistic critique of technique, but the formulation of an objective limit to the design of the supply: the architecture of the service may organize enjoyment, but may not do so as a stable program of exploitation.<1>p. 665</1>
How does the exploitative program become visible?

Exploitation usually operates by accumulation, and it can be described by a vocabulary of dogmatic and evidentiary interest, organized in five families. The first is artificial scarcity and manufactured urgency, with short windows, countdown timers, limited editions and ephemeral events, whose legal effect is to compress the time for reflection and induce hurried consent. The problem is not temporality in the market, but its articulation with opacity and with the practical impossibility of comparing. The minimum signs of proof are time-remaining screens, a history of repeated temporary campaigns and programmed rotation of offers.
The exploitative program does not disappear just because it is spread over small repeated incidents.<1>p. 670</1>

The legally relevant effect lies not only in making the purchase more attractive, but in deliberately compressing the time for reflection and inducing hurried consent, often when essential information remains hidden, scattered or hierarchically demoted.<1>p. 670</1>
The problem is not the isolated use of temporality in the market, but its articulation with opacity and with the practical impossibility of comparison.<1>p. 670</1>

The second is time pressure through events and cycles of promise, with teasers, pre-sales, passes, serial rewards and temporary goals, in which giving up ceases to be an interruption and comes to mean loss of accumulated value and regression of position. With Marques, the consumer appears increasingly captive and less free to resist new impositions. The proof lies in the progression and event rules, in mid-cycle changes and in the comparison between promise and delivery. Azevedo and Torres, dealing with Fortnite, show that this logic may radiate effects onto children, adolescents and families, which confirms the materiality of these techniques, without shifting the axis of the analysis.

The relevant legal effect is the conversion of enjoyment into a directed path, in which giving up ceases to mean a mere interruption of consumption and comes to represent loss of accumulated value, regression of position and discontinuity of an expectation already installed.<1>p. 671</1>

The minimum sign of proof arises in progression structures, event rules, time requirements, modifications introduced mid-cycle and comparison between the initial promise and the actual delivery along the trajectory.<1>p. 671</1>

The combination of the promise of progression, group belonging and marketing integrated into the playful environment shows that capture does not operate only on the abstract individual, but may radiate effects onto children, adolescents and the family unit itself <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 19; p. 10-11; p. 17)</2>.<3>p. 671</3>

The third is the manufacture of risk and the permanent threat of loss, with programmed expiry, opaque banning, loss of access to account or inventory and unintelligible contestation, in which trust is replaced by discipline. The proof comes from the policies applied, sanction notices, the lack of verifiable reasons and decisional inconsistencies. The fourth is the programmed degradation of use value, made of nerfs, the name given to the deliberate weakening of an item, of reconfigurations, of gradual suppressions of function and of the shifting of utility to new layers of acquisition. The object is still there, but worse, and the consumer is pushed to seek substitutes in the same ecosystem. The proof is the functional comparison between before and after, and relevant and repeated erosion is enough, without total suppression.

The consumer no longer chooses in a space of minimum stability and comes to consume under a diffuse threat of deterioration, sanction or partial disappearance of what already forms part of his or her position of enjoyment.<1>p. 672</1>

The minimum sign of proof requires a functional comparison between before and after, examination of relevant versions, identification of the affected core of utility and assessment of the object's role in the experience, exactly as the standard of functional value equivalence already requires. Legal relevance, here, does not depend on total suppression, but on relevant and repeated erosion of enjoyment.<1>p. 672-673</1>

The fifth is existential captivity and identity or social dependence, anchored in inventories, titles, history, ranking, rarities and emblems, in which the loss bears on belonging, recognition and symbolic identity. The proof is not an account of sadness, but the objective demonstration of how the system assigns social value to the object, through internal markers, visibility, participation requirements and reputational effects. None of these techniques is unlawful for existing in the abstract nor for appearing in isolation. They become teleologically abusive when they operate in combination with opacity and permanent asymmetry, in a stable and replicable pattern. This vocabulary, however, is descriptive and operational and does not yet close the qualification, which depends on the test and the framing.

The legal interest here is not to pathologize every intense relationship with the game, but to recognize that the dynamics of retention and reward may function as an objective mechanism for raising the cost of exit and expanding dependence on the continuity of the bond <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 20; p. 21; p. 23-24)</2>.<3>p. 673</3>
Scarcity, urgency, serial promise, threat of loss, functional erosion and symbolic dependence are not unlawful for existing in the abstract nor for appearing in isolation.<1>p. 674</1>

They become teleologically abusive when they operate in combination with opacity and permanent asymmetry, in a stable and replicable pattern, steering enjoyment toward ends incompatible with good faith, balance and controllability of the supply.<1>p. 674</1>
Its role is not yet to close the definitive dogmatic qualification, but to make visible the exploitative program in its recurring forms of manifestation.<1>p. 674</1>
Through which doors of the CDC does the imputation enter?

The category is not worth anything by itself as a claim. Used as a generic label, it indicates no door of the system, legal interest, minimum proof or response, and diluted into episodes, it loses the program. The dilemma between product defect and governance failure is also false, because enjoyment is only consumable through the governance that organizes it, and the same dysfunction appears as a design defect of the mode of supply and as a downgrading of the promised utility. Depending on the structure of the case, abusive teleology may operate as a design defect, when the service is already born architected to produce asymmetry, or as an abusive practice, when everyday governance repeatedly and predictably exploits vulnerability.

The second would be to turn abusive teleology itself into a generic label, incapable of indicating which door of the system was actually triggered, which legal interest was affected, which minimum proof is required and which legal response is adequate.<1>p. 674</1>
The same dysfunction appears, on one side, as a design defect of the mode of supply and, on the other, as a functional or symbolic downgrading of the utility promised to the consumer.<1>p. 666</1>
For this reason, abusive teleology may operate, depending on the structure of the case, as a design defect of the supply and as an abusive practice.<1>p. 668</1>

Counting the doors calls for care. The ordinary doors are three, quality defect, abusive practice and abusive clause, but the safety defect also figures among the doors of the system, because it enters as a shift in borderline cases, from the quality defect, and not as an ordinary axis. The lack of auditability, in turn, is not a fourth door, but a reinforcement of any of the others.
These three doors do not function as watertight compartments.<1>p. 678</1>
Quality defect, safety defect, abusive practice and abusive clause remain the doors of the system.<1>p. 679</1>

The first door is the quality defect, for the relevant loss of adequacy, continuity or functional equivalence. The criterion is not whether the item remains listed in the account, but whether the service, as governed, remains fit for the legitimately expected ends, including when the nonconformity results from the breach of ancillary duties, as Bruno Miragem teaches. Article 18 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> is the central door for a relevant defect in a continuous environment, and Article 20 of the CDC<3><4>2</4></3> allows the consumer to seek termination without penalty or a proportional price reduction when the defect lowers the value of the service. The proof requires reconstructing before and after through version records, documentation of the offer, interface evidence and the history of alterations, with a demonstration of the impact on the core of enjoyment.

Art. 18 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> therefore remains the central door for framing a relevant defect in a continuous environment, now read by the yardstick of functional equivalence and not only by the classic image of the spoiled product on the shelf.<3>p. 562</3>

Faced with quality defects that lower the value of the service, the consumer may demand termination of the contract without penalty or a proportional reduction of the price, with no need to discuss the supplier's fault, since this is strict liability (Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 354<1>p. 563</1>

The shift to the safety defect occurs when the program produces relevant risk or actual harm to goods of a personal dimension, as in the combination of opaque sanctions, severe reputational exclusions, erasure of history, permanent threat of loss and practical impossibility of contesting. The distinction rests on Miragem, for whom the CDC separates the protection of safety from that of adequacy, and on Article 14 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1>, which deals with strict liability for defects in the service. If the core lies in downgraded enjoyment, the lens is that of the quality defect, and if it lies in intolerable risk or harm in a personal dimension, it is that of the safety defect.
If the core of the problem lies in downgraded enjoyment, the main lens will be that of the quality defect.<1>p. 676</1>
If it lies in the production of intolerable risk or harm in a personal dimension, the case shifts to the logic of the safety defect.<1>p. 676</1>
Strict liability for defects in the service and for insufficient or inadequate information<1>p. 520</1>

The second door is the abusive practice, in which teleology appears most strongly as a repeated method. The point of imputation is the pattern, so that scarcity, urgency, cycles of promise, manufactured risk and hindered reversal can be reached even if the service remains available and nothing was literally false. With Benjamin, Marques and Bessa, the practice is linked to irregular conditions of negotiation and to Article 51, item IV, of the CDC<1><2>4</2></1>, which prohibits clauses of exaggerated disadvantage. Article 39 of the CDC<3><4>5</4></3> is linked to dark patterns, with Marques, Mendes and Bergstein, and with emphasis on items IV, V and XII, on taking advantage of the consumer's weakness, demanding a manifestly excessive advantage and leaving performance to the supplier's sole discretion. The proof combines evidence of flow, documentation of campaigns, rules of the ecosystem and records of the decision path, without needing to show that a consumer was psychologically defeated.
The point of imputation, then, is the pattern, not the isolated event.<1>p. 676</1>
The CDC does not require literal falsity to react to this kind of mechanism.<1>p. 676</1>

Art. 51, IV, simultaneously incorporates the principles of objective good faith and economic balance, prohibiting clauses that impose exaggerated disadvantage <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 627)</2>.<3>p. 676</3>
When it is recognized that it is possible to sanction cases of deceptive design and the provisions of art. 39 of the CDC<1><2>5</2></1> are linked<3>p. 432</3>

Art. 39. The supplier of products or services is prohibited, among other abusive practices, from: IV - taking advantage of the consumer's weakness or ignorance […]; V - demanding from the consumer a manifestly excessive advantage; XII - failing to set a deadline for the performance of its obligation or leaving the setting of its starting date to its sole discretion.<1>p. 520</1>
The case need not show that a single consumer was “psychologically defeated” by the system.<1>p. 676</1>

The third door is the abusive clause, when the program gains institutionalization in terms, policies and acceptances, with broad powers of alteration, exclusion, reconfiguration and sanction, without sufficient auditability, real reciprocity or intelligible contestation. With Marques, abusiveness is recognized in the common aim of improving the drafter's position and in the effect of unbalancing the contract, and it is measured by the contract and the performance seen as a dynamic whole. Article 51, item XIII, of the CDC<1><2>6</2></1> makes null the clause that authorizes the supplier to unilaterally alter content or quality after contracting, which does not mean that every alteration is unlawful. The notion of the barrier clause, which Marques traces back to Article 51, item IV, of the CDC<3><4>4</4></3>, reaches trails of multiple authorizations, papers and proofs, without plausible justification, that serve only to discourage the consumer.
When the exploitative program gets a contractual badge, the CDC does not back down.<1>p. 678</1>
Abusiveness, therefore, is not measured only by the contractual sentence taken alone, but by the design of the contract and the performance seen as a dynamic whole.<1>p. 667</1>
A clause that purports to authorize the supplier to alter, at its sole will, the content or quality of the performance after contracting is null<1>p. 562</1>

When performance or reversal only become possible after excessively costly trails, without plausible justification, the very form of organizing the bond already functions as a device for containing the consumer's claim.<1>p. 668</1>

Claudia Lima Marques shows that the “barrier clause” is contrary to art. 51, IV, of the CDC<1><2>4</2></1>, precisely because it substantially unbalances the contractual relationship <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1236)</4>.<5>p. 669</5>

The doors are not compartments, and the framing matrix serves to guide without fragmenting. In each case, one must ask which mechanism predominates, which legal interest was affected, which door offers the main fit, which minimum proof can be required and which remedy is most adequate. Open auditability and functional value equivalence work as cross-cutting filters, because opacity intensifies imputation by practice, aggravates the reading of the clause and weakens the defense of simple adaptation, while the break of equivalence is a strong sign of inadequacy. The response follows the problem. Downgrading tends to call for functional restoration, contractual engineering calls for a consequence on the clause or policy, and the repeated pattern calls for procedural correction and injunctive relief, with support in Article 84 of the CDC<1><2>7</2></1>, which allows the judge to order abstention from or performance of conduct under a coercive order.

In each case, it matters to identify which mechanism predominates, which legal interest was affected, which door of the system offers the main fit, which minimum proof can be required and which remedy is most adequate.<1>p. 678</1>
When the problem lies in the downgrading of enjoyment, the priority tends to fall on the functional restoration of the lost utility.<1>p. 679</1>

When the case reveals a repeated pattern of architectural exploitation, the system also calls for procedural correction and injunctive relief, so as to interrupt the reproduction of the program.<1>p. 679</1>

The judge may, on the basis of art. 84, order abstention from or performance of conduct under the force of a coercive order, precisely because the market must be cleaned up in favor of the consumer and of competition <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 473)</2>.<3>p. 679</3>
How can the regime be examined without atomizing or inflaming the conflict?

The ten guidelines of control move the center of gravity of the examination from clauses and terminal acts to the supply regime, and each follows from the previous one. The first treats architecture and governance as constitutive elements of the supply, and not as a neutral setting, because it is through them that paths, frictions and the conditions in which reaction will be possible are defined. The second subjects relevant alterations to open auditability and functional value equivalence, and not to the generic discourse of updating, so that what matters is whether the change was made intelligible and whether it preserved the function that justified the purchase. The third requires, for private sanctions with material impact, verifiable reasons, decisional coherence and contestation that is not an empty ritual.
The first guideline, therefore, consists in treating architecture and governance not as a neutral setting of the bond, but as constitutive elements of the supply itself.<1>p. 749</1>

The question is whether the alteration was made institutionally intelligible and whether it preserved, in substantial terms, the function that justified the purchase and structured the consumer's legitimate expectation.<1>p. 749</1>
The procedure must be institutionally reconstructable and contestation must not be a mere empty ritual.<1>p. 750</1>

The fourth calls for seeing the case in its trajectory, from the conditions of adhesion, understanding and access to records, because ignoring this is accepting that the supplier also controls the way the conflict will be narrated. The fifth refuses to treat opacity as a neutral trait of digital complexity and recognizes it as a factor that intensifies vulnerability and the asymmetry of proof, which justifies orders to preserve and produce minimum records, delimited expert examinations and dynamic redistribution of the burden, the subject of the chapter on proof. The sixth calls for control specific to the concrete conflict and attentive to structure, separating the individual inadequacy correctable without further expansion from the regime defect, repeatable and built into ordinary operation.
The case, therefore, must be seen in its trajectory and not only in its outcome.<1>p. 750</1>
Opacity, in other words, cannot operate as a procedural privilege self-generated by the governance model itself.<1>p. 750</1>

The institutional challenge lies in recognizing when the case reveals an individual inadequacy correctable without further expansion and when, on the contrary, it exposes a regime defect, repeatable and built into the ordinary mode of operation of the ecosystem.<1>p. 750</1>

The seventh gives preference, whenever possible, to functional restoration and procedural correction, with restoration of access, review of sanctions, restoration of functionality, preservation of history and equivalent replacement, because a money judgment tends to be a poor remedy when what was lost was enjoyment. The eighth opens room, in the face of a repeated, replicable and built-in pattern, for injunctive relief and regime correction, with procedural duties, architectural adjustments and review of sanction flows. The ninth preserves sobriety, because the judge need not become the system's engineer, but rather bring the environment back to verifiable filters of legitimacy. The tenth keeps the unity between supply, proof and remedy, since the way enjoyment is governed conditions the way the conflict is proved and the distribution of access and opacity influences the adequacy of the response.
The complexity of the digital does not eliminate the law.<1>p. 751</1>
The system cannot treat programmatic harms as a casual accumulation of autonomous conflicts.<1>p. 751</1>
Artificially separating these planes produces decisions that are formally organized but materially blind.<1>p. 751-752</1>
Does the contract not authorize the change?
